title: Letter 1
paragraphs: You'll be glad to hear that nothing has gone wrong at the start of this expedition you were so worried about. I arrived here yesterday. My first task is to reassure my dear sister that I'm well and more confident than ever in the success of my venture.

I'm already far north of London. As I walk through the streets of Petersburgh, I feel a cold northern breeze on my cheeks that braces my nerves and fills me with delight. Do you understand this feeling? This wind has traveled from the very regions I'm heading toward, giving me a taste of those icy lands. Inspired by this wind of promise, my daydreams grow more vivid and intense. I try to convince myself that the pole is nothing but frost and emptiness, but my imagination keeps painting it as a place of beauty and wonder. There, Margaret, the sun never sets. Its wide disk skims the horizon, spreading endless light. There — and forgive me, sister, if I trust the navigators who came before me — snow and frost are banished. We may sail over calm seas to a land more wondrous than any yet discovered. What it produces and how it looks may be unlike anything known, just as the phenomena of the heavens undoubtedly are in those unexplored regions. What might we find in a country of eternal light? I may discover the mysterious force that draws the compass needle. I may bring order to a thousand astronomical observations whose apparent irregularities need only this voyage to be explained for good. I'll see parts of the world no one has ever visited. I may walk on land no human foot has ever touched. These are my enticements. They're enough to conquer any fear of danger or death. They make me begin this difficult voyage with the joy a child feels setting out in a little boat with his holiday friends to explore the river near his home. And even if all my theories prove wrong, you can't deny the enormous benefit I'll bring to all of humanity, down to the last generation, by discovering a passage near the pole to those countries that now take so many months to reach, or by unlocking the secret of the magnet — something that, if it can be done at all, can only be achieved by an expedition like mine.

These thoughts have calmed the anxiety I felt when I started this letter. My heart glows with an enthusiasm that lifts me to heaven, because nothing calms the mind like having a steady purpose — a fixed point on which the soul can focus. This expedition has been my dream since childhood. I devoured every account of voyages toward the North Pacific through the polar seas. You may remember that our good Uncle Thomas's entire library consisted of histories of voyages of discovery. My education was neglected, but I was passionately fond of reading. Those books were my constant study, day and night. They deepened the regret I'd felt as a child when I learned that my father's dying wish had forbidden my uncle from letting me go to sea.

Those dreams faded when I first read the great poets, whose words entranced my soul and lifted it to heaven. I became a poet myself and lived for a year in a paradise of my own making. I imagined I might earn a place in the temple where Homer and Shakespeare are honored. You know well how I failed and how heavily I bore the disappointment. But just at that time I inherited my cousin's fortune, and my thoughts turned back to their earlier direction.

Six years have passed since I committed myself to this great enterprise. I can still remember the exact hour when I dedicated myself to it. I began by toughening my body against hardship. I joined whale-fishers on several expeditions to the North Sea. I voluntarily endured cold, hunger, thirst, and sleeplessness. I often worked harder than the common sailors during the day and spent my nights studying mathematics, medicine, and the branches of science most useful to a naval adventurer. Twice I actually hired myself out as an under-mate on a Greenland whaler and performed admirably. I must admit I felt a little proud when my captain offered me the second-highest position on the vessel and begged me to stay, so valuable did he find my services.

And now, dear Margaret, don't I deserve to accomplish something great? I could have lived in ease and luxury, but I chose glory over every comfort that wealth offered me. Oh, if only some encouraging voice would say yes! My courage and resolution are firm, but my hopes waver, and my spirits often sink. I'm about to set out on a long and difficult voyage that will demand all my strength. I must not only lift the spirits of others but sometimes sustain my own when theirs are failing.

This is the best time to travel in Russia. The sledges fly quickly over the snow. The motion is pleasant — far more comfortable than an English stagecoach, in my opinion. The cold isn't unbearable if you wrap yourself in furs, a habit I've already adopted. There's a huge difference between walking on deck and sitting motionless for hours, when no exercise keeps the blood from actually freezing in your veins. I have no desire to die on the road between St. Petersburgh and Archangel.

I'll leave for Archangel in two or three weeks. I plan to hire a ship there — easily done by paying the owner's insurance — and to recruit as many experienced whale-fishermen as I need. I don't intend to sail until June. And when shall I return? Ah, dear sister, how can I answer that? If I succeed, many, many months, perhaps years, will pass before we meet again. If I fail, you'll see me again soon, or never.
Farewell, my dear, excellent Margaret. May heaven shower blessings on you and keep me safe, so that I may show my gratitude again and again for all your love and kindness.
